name: Antibiotics (doxycycline) for back acne

lead: Doxycycline is a tetracycline-class antibiotic prescribed for moderate to severe inflammatory acne, including on the back and chest, to clear inflamed lesions and reduce the marks they leave.

It blocks bacterial protein synthesis, and anti-inflammatory effects are also thought to contribute, which is why lower sub-antimicrobial doses are used in acne and rosacea. Dermatology guidance cited on Wikipedia describes oral antibiotics as faster-acting than topicals for inflamed lesions.

paras: It is a prescription oral course, usually used alongside topical treatments such as benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid, and commonly for cases where topicals alone have not been enough. Guidance generally recommends limiting courses to about three months.

Common effects include nausea, diarrhoea and increased sunburn risk. Pill esophagitis can occur if swallowed with too little fluid, and use with isotretinoin or other retinoids is contraindicated because of intracranial hypertension risk. The US label warns of tooth discoloration during tooth development and pregnancy concerns, and prolonged use is associated with antibiotic-resistant skin bacteria. It is prescription-only in the US and UK.

angle.text: Doxycycline lowers skin bacteria and inflammation, so inflamed back and body acne lesions clear and leave fewer marks. It is a prescribed acne treatment, with guidelines favouring short courses alongside non-antibiotic treatments.

lead: Doxycycline is a synthetic, broad-spectrum antibiotic of the tetracycline class, developed by Pfizer and first marketed as Vibramycin in 1967.[1][2] It treats a wide range of bacterial infections and is also prescribed for moderate to severe acne vulgaris.[1][3]

In appearance communities it is discussed as an oral treatment for inflammatory acne on the back, chest and shoulders (often called truncal acne or "bacne"), typically for cases where topical products have not been enough. Its acne benefit is attributed partly to anti-inflammatory effects in addition to its action against bacteria.[2]

Dermatology guidance summarised on Wikipedia describes oral antibiotics as faster-acting than topical ones for inflamed lesions, but recommends limiting courses to about three months and pairing them with benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid to limit bacterial resistance.[4] Doxycycline is prescription-only in the United States and United Kingdom.[2]
infobox: Not recommended; former FDA category D

paras: Doxycycline is indicated for respiratory, skin and soft-tissue, eye and sexually transmitted infections, rickettsial and tick-borne diseases, malaria prophylaxis and other conditions, and the US label lists adjunctive use in severe acne.[1][2][3]

Acne on the trunk is treated with the same drug classes as facial acne. Wikipedia's acne article notes that oral antibiotics, including tetracyclines, are commonly prescribed for moderate to severe inflammatory acne, though it does not give guidance specific to back acne.[4]

Subantimicrobial-dose doxycycline is also used for acne and rosacea; studies cited on Wikipedia suggest it works without inducing antibiotic resistance, although the exact mechanism is not fully understood.[2] Low-dose regimens (40 mg daily) are described there as appearing about as effective as 100 mg with fewer gastrointestinal effects, and are not FDA-approved for acne.[4]

Wikipedia's acne article reports that oral antibiotics are generally more effective than topical ones and bring faster resolution of inflammatory lesions, with a 2014 review finding them somewhat more effective than birth control pills at three months and about equal at six months.[4] Improvement is generally seen 8 to 12 weeks after starting therapy.[4]

Guidelines referenced there recommend that oral antibiotics be used for no longer than three months, preferably as part of combination therapy, and not together with a topical antibiotic.[4] Antibiotic overuse has been linked to higher rates of tetracycline-resistant Cutibacterium acnes.[4] Despite guideline calls to reduce their use, oral antibiotics remain the most commonly prescribed systemic acne therapy.[4]

Common effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain and increased sunburn (photosensitivity); rash on sun-exposed skin has been reported in roughly 7 to 21 percent of people taking it for malaria prophylaxis.[2] Pill esophagitis can occur when tablets are taken with insufficient fluid.[2][3]

Rare or serious effects listed include hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, increased intracranial pressure and Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea.[1][3] It is contraindicated with isotretinoin and other retinoids because both can rarely cause intracranial hypertension.[2] A large retrospective study cited on Wikipedia found a 2.25-fold higher risk of Crohn's disease in people treated for acne.[2]

The US label states that tetracycline-class drugs given during tooth development (late pregnancy, infancy and childhood up to age 8) may cause permanent tooth discoloration, and that there are no adequate controlled studies in pregnant women.[3] Doxycycline is not recommended in pregnancy and passes into breast milk.[2]

Doxycycline binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and inhibits bacterial protein synthesis, giving a bacteriostatic effect.[1] Compared with earlier tetracyclines it is almost completely absorbed orally and has a longer half-life, allowing once- or twice-daily dosing.[1] Its benefit in acne and rosacea is thought to involve anti-inflammatory and anti-angiogenic effects as well.[2]

Chlortetracycline, the first tetracycline antibiotic, was discovered at American Cyanamid in the late 1940s. Doxycycline was created at Pfizer as a more stable and effective analogue, patented in 1957, developed clinically in the early 1960s and approved by the FDA in 1967.[2]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a completed phase 4 registration comparing Doryx (delayed-release doxycycline) tablets with doxycycline hyclate in 93 people with acne vulgaris, started in 2008; the registry entry as reviewed here does not report results and the trial was not specific to back acne.[5] Controlled trial evidence specific to doxycycline for back or truncal acne was not found; the general acne evidence summarised above comes from reviews of facial and mixed-site acne.[4]

Doxycycline is a generic medicine sold under many brand names, including Vibramycin and Doryx.[2] In looksmaxxing and skin-care communities, back acne is often discussed as a cosmetic concern that people raise with dermatologists, and oral antibiotics are one of the options mentioned alongside topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide and isotretinoin. No community-specific protocols are described here.
